The government statement also expresses economic optimism, while giving uncertainty as another reason for restraint. Neither shows that anticipated financial rewards prevented a broad moratorium. limitations: Public statements may omit motives or present them selectively.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: The apparent economics of AI, which may or may not come to pass as imagined, are too seductive to too many people (AI company builders, investors, people paid 6- and 7-digit salaries, and those expecting big-tech campaign donations) for any AI moratorium to happen in the near term.
conditions: we will see if they yet come to pass as imagined

statement.excerpt: The apparent economics of AI (we will see if they yet come to pass as imagined) are too seductive to too many, to people building AI companies, to people investing in AI companies, to people getting paid 6 and even 7 digit salaries, and to people expecting campaign donations from big tech companies.
statement.document_title: Six months after the Pause letter, AI is still erratic — and still something we should still be deeply concerned about

from_speaker: we will see if they yet come to pass as imagined
people getting paid 6 and even 7 digit salaries
people expecting campaign donations from big tech companies
our_interpretation: Read with the preceding sentence, Marcus attributes the failure to secure a near-term moratorium to anticipated financial rewards among developers, investors, employees, and political recipients.
The testable plain reading is that those incentives materially prevented agreement on a broad frontier-development pause.
The parenthetical hedges eventual profitability. It is not an antecedent requiring those profits to materialize before the causal claim can be assessed.
This is a claim about incentives and political causation, not a specified company financial metric or a separate salary estimate.
“Near-term” remains unbounded; later records may illuminate the mechanism but do not establish a deadline.
criteria.support_condition: Decision records, documented lobbying effects, or credible comparative studies show that anticipated financial rewards materially caused relevant actors to reject or block a broad moratorium.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Comparable decision evidence shows that the asserted incentives did not materially block agreement, or a broad moratorium was agreed during the relevant period despite those incentives.

evidence.locator: First policy section, following the statement that the UK would not rush to regulate
evidence.explanation: Sunak’s speech combines economic optimism with uncertainty about how to regulate AI. This supplies a stated alternative explanation for restraint, but neither establishes his complete motives nor resolves the cause of a broad moratorium’s absence.

public_payload.what_would_resolve: Contemporaneous deliberations or corroborated causal research connecting financial incentives to rejection of a specific broad moratorium, with competing explanations examined.
